text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a subject close to all of our hearts, food. And in particular,
the politics of food. It was a discussion I chaired at this year's Sydney Writers
Festival. And before we got going I was fascinated to know what the audience's
attitudes were to food, and I found that most of them were on a gluten-free diet,
and a large proportion were watching their carbs.

Anyway, on the panel were Indira Naidoo, author of The Edible Balcony and The
Edible City, Damon Gameau, author of That Sugar Book and producer and host
of That Sugar Film, and Julian Baggini, a British philosopher and prolific writer,
including The Virtues of the Table and The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten.

What do you think about people being food focused, Julian? You've got strong
opinions about that.

Julian Baggini: Well, I don't have strong opinions…

Norman Swan: Well, you wrote a book about it.

Julian Baggini: Yes, I did write a book about it, yeah. My philosophical
influences are people like Aristotle and David Hume who actually had very little to
say about food. But if you go to Aristotle, Aristotle advocated this doctrine of the
mean, which is actually funnily enough Confucius also advocated something
similar, and that way of looking at things says that generally speaking the
extremist positions tend to be wrong, and the appropriate thing is something
between.

I think the Western philosophical tradition has tended to be really down on food
and on the body and tended to think that anyone who pays any attention to it at
all is kind of deluded. You know, they are just like animals because animals eat,
so if you focus on eating you're like an animal. Brillat-Savarin, the French food
writer, said animals feed and humans eat. Food is a very important part of life. It's
part of what makes us human, it's very humanising, and it connects us to all sorts
of important issues.

At the same time though, to become obsessive about food, there are certain food
obsessions that I think are legitimate. You know, if you are a really creative chef,
for example, or you are a really great producer of food, that's your obsession, but
 
there are unhealthy obsessions around food, for sure. So it's about finding the
appropriate balance for it in life, the appropriate place for it. It's neither everything
nor nothing.

Norman Swan: The Edible City is all about bringing people together around
food, isn't it.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, it is, and I'm certainly of the school of thought…the first thing
I think about what I wake up in the morning is what I'm going to eat, and the last
thing I think about is what I'm going to eat the next day…

Norman Swan: And in between times? Is there any time you don't think about
food?

Indira Naidoo: I tend to eat about two or three times a day. But for me, food is
much more than a really important part of our life. One of the tragedies we've
fallen into in the Western modern way of looking at food is that it's something
we've developed these paranoias about. 'Oh my God, what is that going to do to
me if I eat that?' And so that has been a really concerning because for me it's a
joyous experience. Food is joyous to eat. The anticipation of food, the sharing of
food, the actual process of eating it and then the discussion around it. So for me
it's a sad day when food isn't the central part of the day. And I think that that is
where it has become really disturbing, is that it's this also-ran thing, this thing I
just pick up on the way or pull out a packet or pour something out of a tin or a
container. I think that that's where the problems have become, that we have
reduced food rather than elevated it to where it should be.

Norman Swan: But do you think Damon has reduced food and created all sorts
of paranoia through his bestselling books?

Damon Gameau: You can answer honestly, it's fine.

Norman Swan: Do you think so?

Indira Naidoo: Look, I think in terms of the Damon's work and Damon's book,
obviously I'm very concerned about the amount of sugar in our diet and I think
that it is a big problem. We are eating something like 1,000% more sugar than
we did 200 years ago. It's leading to lots of disease and wellness issues.
 
Norman Swan: What are you going to do about your desert menus if you
abandon sugar?

Indira Naidoo: Well, I think that we went through the stage when we demonised
fat, we went through the stage when we demonised protein, and I think that we
have to be aware that there are some things we need to have in moderation, like
sugar. But you can't look at food in terms of just its nutrients, you have to look at
it holistically, look at the apple, not just look at it as a sum of proteins and
nutrients and fats and sugars. And I think that that is where we are going a little
wrong.

Norman Swan: So Damon, I've got a bone to pick with you…

Damon Gameau: Pick away.

Norman Swan: Last night I tried one of your recipes. I almost sliced my finger
chopping broccoli.

Damon Gameau: Oh, so I'm to blame! You need to improve your culinary skills.

Norman Swan: I do, refine that technique. Were you surprised by the polling of
the audience in terms of the food obsessions in the audience or food interest?

Damon Gameau: Well, I think we've got to be very careful, I think what we are in
the middle of at the moment is the food revolution where people are starting to
empower themselves with information about food. I don't necessarily think that's
a bad thing as long as it stays in a safe area. I think we have been misled for 35
years in a lot of different ways. I think the environment has supported companies
making enormous amount of profit telling us what to eat and shaping their
marketing strategies to get us hooked on these kind of products.

And certainly where I come from is that we don't think sugar per se is bad or evil,
we are trying to get people to say, look, the World Health Organisation
recommends about six teaspoons of sugar a day. Our teenagers are having
about 40 teaspoons. So clearly there is a lack of understanding with the food
supply. So how do we teach people those skills to raise their awareness, learn to
read labels, understand what they are putting in their bodies, because I think now
the science tells us not only the physical symptoms but your mental, your vitality,
 
your emotions are determined by the foods you are eating. If we can get this
through to kids we're going to set them up for a much healthier lifestyle. And
that's not to say that we demonise these foods, we just get them to take
responsibility and understand what they are putting in their bodies.

Norman Swan: So do you think that you can actually counter the effect of the
globalised food industry?

Damon Gameau: Well, I think we are going to have to because the reality is we
are using nearly 40% of our land now for farming, we are going to be 9 billion
people by 2050, we need to rethink the way we approach food, and I think that's
going to switch us back to local. We are going to have to teach kids about
growing their own vegetables because we can't keep going the way we are. So
we need people to understand food a bit more.

I think the key with sugar is that we forget that sugar is not a nutrient. There is no
biological requirement for added sugar in our diet. We can get all the sugar we
need from fruits and vegetables and other sources. So as a treat, fantastic, every
now and again. But we've got to a point where it is now in 80% of the food supply
and most people are having 30 or 40 teaspoons a day. That's not a treat any
more, that has kind of tipped the balance, and that's why we are seeing this
catastrophic health crisis.

Julian Baggini: Yes, because there's not really a food industry…because I think
sometimes the food industry is presented as this huge, big, all-powerful demon
which excites huge control over us, and of course there have been abuses. And
Damon's film points to the way in which there has been some misinformation and
deliberate suppression of information about the health of this food. So clearly I'm
not saying they are blameless, but I think that the danger of putting that kind of
view of the food industry is it makes it seem like we are less powerful than we
are. And also we got to remember at the end of the day they are about making
money. At the end of the day it's consumer demand. When consumers start
demanding organic, they stock the organic. When they want reduced sugar, they
stock reduced sugar. So they are not going to foist these things upon us if we
don't willingly take them. With more information, we make our choices, the food
industry will respond.
 
Norman Swan: But isn't that a bit naive because what we have is a saturated fat
mountain, we have a sugar mountain. All the food that people don't eat gets put
into a mountain and then put into high calorie, low value foods. There is a degree
of dumping and creation of markets too.

Julian Baggini: Well, there is, but remember, people aren't entirely powerless
about that, except…and this is where it gets very interesting, the politics…of
course where people are poor, where there is not enough money. So I think in
developed countries most people actually have the resources to eat proper good
food, it's often not more expensive if you know where to get it. But let's be
honest, generally speaking you do have to pay a bit to get the quality stuff. Most
people can afford that, they choose other priorities, it's as simple as that. But
there's always that 10%, 20% of people in countries like Australia, in Britain, who
have very little money, and those are the people who have very little choice but
to buy those processed products with all these things in it. So that's where the
politics I think it gets more tricky.

Indira Naidoo: I agree with Julian in terms of the food companies do respond to
consumers. I mean, in the end they are there to make money, and if consumers
want a particular product with a particular composition, they will respond to it. We
have seen examples of that here in Australia. My concern is when consumers
show that they want a certain product…for instance, we are having a big debate
in Australia at the moment with our free range eggs. Consumers have shown that
they want free range eggs but they want them to be labelled accurately. And
unfortunately the policy makers aren't helping consumers make that decision. So
eggs are being labelled as free range when…

Norman Swan: They are just in a larger cage.

Indira Naidoo: Exactly, 10,000 chickens to a shed instead of the 1,500, which is
the code. This makes it really hard for consumers. They want to do the right
thing, they want to buy free range, but they are presented with a product that
clearly is not. And what that does is the people who are doing the right thing, the
egg farmers who are doing the right thing, looking after those animals well and
delivering a free range product, are getting messed up in the caged hens and the
limited access to outdoor pasture. So that's why for me it needs to be a two-
pronged approach. Consumers, yes, say we now have got the information, this is
 
what we want. The companies say, okay, we will respond to that. But the
policymakers have to make sure that those regulations are enforced and the
people who do the wrong thing are punished.

Damon Gameau: And the problem in Australia that we found with the film is
that…we've had two UK parliamentary screenings, New Zealand parliamentary
screening, we had two scheduled in Australia, and not one politician turned up,
didn't even send an intern. I got to go and meet one of the ministers, and we are
the second biggest exporter of sugar in the world, so it's kind of a don't-go-there
topic. And at the same time, look, there are a host of factors that are contributing
to the diseases we're seeing but sugar is a major factor, especially around kids,
that if they had the gumption to actually take some…I agree, it's part empowering
the consumer but also the government need to help out in some way, whether it's
regulating the companies, but they need to take action.

Norman Swan: So it has been said that big food is acting like a big tobacco now.
One of the things that we know works with tobacco, and particularly in children, is
price. Where do you stand on a sugar tax?

Damon Gameau: Well, I guess the only working model of it so far has come out
of Mexico and it has now been 18 months, they put a levy on sugary drinks,
they've seen a 17% reduction in their lower socio-economic areas. But more
importantly they've raised $1.8 billion. So the only way I would support it (and I
don't think this is going to happen) is if we set up a transparent independent body
that said, all right, with that money raised, let's use it to subsidise fresh fruits and
vegetables, let's revamp our hospital system and our schools and give them
fresh, affordable foods. But unfortunately I don't think we are going to see that
happen, it's going to disappear into the coffers.

Norman Swan: A new submarine in South Australia.

Damon Gameau: There you go, yes.

Norman Swan: But then people will say it's the Nanny State. People have got
control over their lives, Julian, let it be.

Julian Baggini: Nanny State arguments are very easy to make. The fact of the
matter is that we support regulation of all sorts of things for our mutual benefit. It
 
is not a nanny because if the restrictions are there with the consent and the
approval and demand of the populace, it is something we choose together, it's
not about the state saying 'you can't do that'. But also I think the other problem
with the Nanny State argument is we've got to remember that the people who
make that case, imagine that there is something out there which is called the
pure free market which is operating independently of any government on policy
issues, and that that is sufficient. That is not the case and it never has been the
case. We have the kind of foods we have in the proportion we have them at the
price we have them for all sorts of very complicated issues around agricultural
subsidy, trade tariffs and so forth. The food supply system is saturated in policy
and law and regulation. So when someone says what we are going to do is we
want to change a part of that to get slightly better results, you're not introducing
an intervention which wasn't there before, you are simply changing what exactly
is being intervened about. So it's perfectly legitimate.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, I agree absolutely. We do tend to forget that government
policy has led us to where we are in our food system at the moment. It hasn't
happened separate to government policy, they have been actively intervening in
that process over the last 10, 20, 30 years. And also too you've got to remember
that the food companies are actively intervening as well. Every couple of months
they are changing compositions of foods to amp up sugar or amp up salt or fat.
So the whole system…it's not that you are just being given a product that just sits
there and hasn't been changed in a number of decades, everyone involved in this
process is changing compositions. And unfortunately in terms of government
policy and health policy we've been lagging behind, we have not been keeping
up with how willing big business is to change the composition of foods to make it
almost impossible not to be addictive. Our brains love salt, fat and sugar. Who in
this room doesn't love that!

Norman Swan: You're listening to a discussion on the politics of food from this
year's Sydney Writers Festival. On the panel are Indira Naidoo, Damon Gameau,
and philosopher Julian Baggini.

I want to get back to a comment that Damon made right at the beginning which is
the back to the earth idea of growing your own food, which you give I think four
examples in The Edible City, a couple in Melbourne and Sydney, Wayside
Chapel and so on. But to what extent is it scalable? We are trying to limit the size
 
of our cities, lose the quarter-acre block, live in apartments. I know you've got the
balcony idea. But nonetheless, how practical is it that we can get back in touch
with our food?

Indira Naidoo: I think we really need to. We have all become grossly
disconnected from our food. And the groups I particularly work with are the ones
that are suffering most from this new food world. You know, they are poor,
disadvantaged, homeless, newly arrived immigrants, asylum seekers, elderly,
retired, kids in school. So they are the people unfortunately that so many of these
bad products are being directed at. And what I found from my work is when you
help these communities reconnect with their food, even if it's just growing a few
pots of herbs on their balcony or on the stairwell or if they have a balcony or a a
little garden, that process of seeing how something grows, to see a piece of fruit,
to see a lettuce, a cabbage, an apple actually grow, has been quite
transformative for so many of these communities because something like 60% of
our diet…

Norman Swan: But in the end it's cheaper to buy something from the burger
shop down the road.

Indira Naidoo: Well, you have to educate people about what cheap actually
means. And I think that we've gone through an era where we expect food to be
cheap, but what we don't understand is that so many of the external costs of that
food haven't actually been priced into the cost of that food.

Norman Swan: So the food miles, the transportation…

Indira Naidoo: That's right. So a McDonald's hamburger may cost three dollars,
but when you look at the food miles, the environmental aspect, the low wages
paid to workers, the cost of pollution, whatever it might be, if you really put all
those costs into the value of the hamburger, actually the average person
probably wouldn't be able to afford it.

Norman Swan: But isn't that slightly naive because you should have it costed
into the price of the hamburger but it's not, and if you haven't got much money
then that's what your money goes on.
 
Indira Naidoo: Absolutely. I mean, I'm not someone who is anti-hamburgers
particularly, but it's about what you help people get access to. And in the suburbs
I work in, sometimes fast food is the only thing they have. There's no grocery
stores, not even a general supermarket. So you have to work within that. But
once you introduce that sense that they can have a little bit of autonomy, see
how food grows, what it takes to grow food, it starts making them think differently.
So when you buy an eggplant for 5c or 10c at the supermarket and it has taken
you three months to grow it, you ask different questions as a conscious
consumer and eater than you would as just a consumer. And I think that that is
part of the process. Obviously no one is going to be able to grow all the food they
need when you live in urban environments in cities, but we can certainly grow
much more of our food, we can localise it much more, make it more nutritious
and more accessible, and also cheaper.

Our homeless community in the Wayside Chapel in Potts Point I work with, 200
square metres on that rooftop we grow vegetables, we have five or six beehives
producing honey. And when our homeless visitors arrive in the garden every
Thursday for garden class, the first thing they do is literally eat the garden. That
is their meal of the day. And the first time that happened it really blew me away
because obviously they don't have the income to buy nutritious food, and for
them that vegetable garden is their supermarket.

Norman Swan: So how to do these adjustments, Damon?

Damon Gameau: I kind of agree with Indira in the sense that we are not going to
have a choice. I think we are going to have to switch to this kind of micro farming,
food towers, we are going to have to start growing more local. And the
Worldwatch Institute did a report that said that 80% of New York residents could
be fed from rooftop gardens. And the way we are heading, the impact on our
food and our apples being shipped from London to South Africa to be polished
and then shipped back to the UK to be sold, it's absolutely mad. We need to find
a way to promote local eating again. And, as Indira was saying, I think a burger
should be reflective of what its true value is in terms of those miles. So if you
want a hamburger, great, but it's going to be $11. But if you want the local
banana, is going to be 40c because…

Norman Swan: So that implies differential taxation by governments.
 
Damon Gameau: Well, I think it's inevitable. We don't realise the impact of
what's happening to our climate. I don't think people understand how food is
going to be affected in the next 40 to 50 years. We are going to have to make
some fundamental decisions around that because we cannot keep going the way
we are. So I think the more we can force people to try and grow their own, have
these community gardens, it's going to help.

Julian Baggini: I've got reservations about all of this. I think that it's always good
to grow food for various reasons, not mainly around self-sufficiency I would say
actually, to do with other things, connection and stuff. But I think there's a bit of a
danger of turning this local thing into a kind of religion, and it doesn't add up
actually. I think there are really good things about eating things that are not
remotely local, for all sorts of reasons. First of all, I grew up in a time where the
progressive view was always one of internationalism and connections with other
people, and I think that part of the way we have food from all around the world is
part of that more cosmopolitan, outward looking thing. And I worry in Britain
sometimes…

Norman Swan: Not many mango trees in Glasgow, I can tell you.

Julian Baggini: No, exactly. And so sometimes this 'go local' thing in Britain,
what bothers me is it is happening as a cultural phenomenon at about the same
sort of time where people are also talking about closing the borders, keeping the
immigrants out et cetera. It's the benign side, it can be, not always, an element of
it is a benign side of a kind of provincialism. But also on environmental grounds
it's not as straightforward as 'local is better'.

Interesting reports done on New Zealand's products, New Zealand has lamb and
butter and everything. They can produce it with a very low carbon footprint
because they've got the perfect environment for it. And shipping is a very, very
low carbon way of transferring things. The total carbon footprint of something
grown in optimal conditions and shipped very far distance can be less than
something grown locally where you have to put a lot of synthetic inputs, artificial
heating, greenhouses and so forth.

So I'm all for lots of getting back in touch with the local and supporting it and
certainly avoiding foods which carry this very, very heavy carbon footprint, but it's
 
just too simplistic to think that everything that has travelled a long way has a
heavy carbon footprint. It doesn't. Bananas are great. And bananas, they don't
grow here, we put them in ships, low carbon footprint, delicious, nutritious. And,
even when fair trade, not very expensive.

Damon Gameau: How do you think that looks when we have 10 billion people in
2050 and an estimated 28 billion by the end of the century? How do we deal with
those trade routes and shipping? If we are still existing as we are now, what are
the implications for the planet?

Julian Baggini: Well, they will have to be changes for various reasons, as the
one you pointed out. But I think the solution for our food security is not to reduce
our interdependence. We are going to become more interdependent. In a
globalised world it's even more important that we trade in ways that are efficient,
that we grow things where they grow best and most efficiently, and where we can
transport them with a low carbon footprint we can. If we try and grow everything
local to us, then what's going to happen is that people who are blessed with the
climates and everything that they can do that will do well, and other people are
going to starve, so we have to make these adjustments.

Norman Swan: Let's try this bit of moral calculus on you. So the National Party in
Australia, the country party, objects, by and large, to foreign interests buying our
farming land. A huge debate over a very large livestock holding recently which
the government caved in on and said, well, they couldn't buy it with the way it
was structured. And the theory here is that, well, dairy produce, meat produce is
going to be grown and sent straight to China, and then we might be having a
problem with food security. What's the moral calculus around this? Have the
Chinese got a right to buy our agricultural land, export directly to China, in a
growing world which, if Damon is right, we're going to need every scrap of food
we can get?

Julian Baggini: Look, there are lots of issues tied up in that. When it comes to
land ownership we have a system where people can privately own land, but it
doesn't mean that once you've paid for it it's yours and you can do what you like
with it. Without knowing the ins and outs of this particular debate, who owns it or
not in a legal contract isn't really the key issue. The main thing is there are
regulations in any given country about how land is used so it's used in a
 
sustainable and fair way and it benefits everybody and it benefits the people here
as well.

Indira Naidoo: This debate has concerned me a little because I find sometimes
it's a little racist. It's always the Chinese. And there are a lot of other foreign
investors who are buying up Australian land and Australian dairies and
agricultural land. So I'd like to see just more about foreign interests rather than a
particular nationality.

But I think this is the important thing about the education process about growing
food, is that you see the importance of our food producers and our growers in the
system. And again, when you are an urban consumer going to the supermarket,
you are not really thinking about where that food comes from, who has grown it,
who has put all that effort into it. And when you grow an eggplant and you
understand the time, the effort, the commitment, the people who do that fulltime
become your heroes. And I think that this debate hopefully is repositioning our
farmers in a more positive and strong light, because without them, who is going
to grow our food?

Norman Swan: So we are seeing a dairy crisis as we speak?

Indira Naidoo: We are.

Norman Swan: Julian sits on an organisation called the Food Ethics Council in
the UK and they talk about a square deal for farmers. Do you think we are giving
Australian farmers a square deal?

Indira Naidoo: No, of course not. I mean, we are seeing the death of our rural
communities, farmers now walking off the land. We are seeing hugely high
suicide rates amongst our farming community. I think it's devastating. I don't
know how farmers are hanging in there. But I think we need to bridge this urban
and rural gap that we've got at the moment. And I think food and understanding
the importance of it and how important that food is going to become for our
future…Australia is becoming more and more climate challenged. We have only
got a really thin fertile strip around the edge of our country to grow food, and the
people who can do it well and do it productively are really key to the future of our
country.
 
Damon Gameau: Yes, I think a symptom of that too is that most people are
unaware that I think 80c of every dollar that Australians spend goes to either
Coles or Woollies, whether it's through food, alcohol, gambling, petrol. So it's
almost a dictatorship in a way. And I think because of that impact, the way they
can affect the farmers there…I've met a farmer who grows lettuce, and he said
his quota that he has to provide every month is 1,000 tonnes of lettuce. Now, he
has to grow that amount every single month. If a company only wants 400
tonnes, then that 600 tonnes gets thrown out. So the system is just so
unproductive the way we are doing it at the moment, and this is where we need
to rethink how we are approaching this. And ultimately it's probably a systemic
problem that, as you said, we've designed a system that…

Norman Swan: But in the end it's a market and in the end you've got to change
the way the the market works. So tell me how you would change…

Indira Naidoo: But I think you've also got to help consumers make a much more
informed question. I worked at Choice, a consumer advocacy group, and I was
really fascinated by the main question that consumers ask themselves when they
go into a shop; how much does something cost. That was their first question.

Norman Swan: And if you talk to Coles and Woollies, that's what they say, it's
price, price, price.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, and obviously it is not always the best question. And so
what I hope we can help people do is ask the other questions they need to ask;
why does it cost that, why doesn't it cost this, who has made it, what's gone into
it, how has it been produced, how are those animals being treated? There are a
whole lot of other questions. When you get a litre of milk the same or cheaper
than a litre of water, you know something has gone wrong. As a consumer you
shouldn't go, 'yay, that's fantastic', you should say 'someone has been screwed-
over here'.

Norman Swan: And it's the water buyers! Damon, how do you square your view
about food miles with, if you like, social justice across nations where coffee
producers, cocoa producers, and increasingly others…as sub-Saharan Africa
gets a bit richer, they'll start producing grain and other things, drought
 
allowing…don't they have a right to sell their products on an international market
and ship them to distant places?

Damon Gameau: Of course, and I think what we are losing here is we are
switching to extremities. We are not saying that suddenly we stop all trade and
shipping. If there are certain things that still require that and they are available at
a certain price because they are a special, yes, absolutely. But like I said, when
we are shipping apples between countries for no reason other than the polishing,
I think there's a broken system there, because it's cheaper to do that for them
than do it within their own country, that's the issue we need to address.

Norman Swan: But what I'm losing here in this discussion is (I'm sorry, I'm being
boring and practical) how are you adjust the market so that it's different for
apples from coffee.

Julian Baggini: Look, it is really, really difficult, I think this is true. The thing
about the market system, the so-called perfection of the market, is that there is a
lot of truth involved in it. One reason why it's good to have trade is that it's more
efficient for some people to do a lot of one thing rather than everyone doing
everything themselves. An apple tree in every garden is not as efficient as an
orchard from which we all take things. So there is no simple answer. Food is also
complicated because supply is not easily switched on and off because there are
all sorts of things to do with the weather and the seasons this year and
everything. So getting it perfectly right is very difficult.

I think the point is you shouldn't be seduced by the idea of what would the perfect
system look like. I think we can see lots of examples already where systems
have emerged for various usually political reasons which just have bizarre and
perverse consequences…

Norman Swan: Such as?

Julian Baggini: Subsidies, for example, for grain. It is particularly bad in
America. America subsidises the production of certain crops…

Norman Swan: Fructose is the classic one.
 
Julian Baggini: Yes, exactly, which creates this glut of fructose which means it
has to be put into everything and corn syrup and everything. So there are lots of
perverse incentives there. And there is also not the right kind of taxation. We put
taxation on things and we have very crude categories for this. You know, luxury
goods get sales tax in the UK, basic foodstuffs don't. But what fits into what
category? It varies.

So I think in a way there is nothing really simple and inspiring that we can say
about this. We have to go ad hoc, bit by bit, changing this bit of regulation, that
regulation, trying to nudge ourselves towards something, and also having the
humility to realise that this is a bit experimental. Markets and food supply
systems are extremely complicated and there's always the risk of unintentionally
having a perverse outcome.

People with perfectly good intentions…in the EU for example, after the Second
World War the EU decided it had to make sure it never got close to starvation
again because during the war lots of people got close to starvation. So it had
these agricultural policies designed to create food security, but because they
were, in retrospect, badly designed, it just created the butter lakes, the milk
lakes, the butter mountains. So we've got to have the humility to realise that we
may well get things like this wrong. But you've got to at least start with an
awareness of what the proper problem is and what we are trying to get towards.
And I think at the moment, up until now perhaps too much has been based on
the idea…the main incentive is to keep things cheap and that's it.

Norman Swan: That was part of a discussion on the politics of food that I chaired
at this year's Writers Festival. You were listening to Indira Naidoo, author of The
Edible Balcony and The Edible City, Damon Gameau, author of That Sugar
Book and That Sugar Film, and Julian Baggini, a British philosopher and prolific
writer, including The Virtues of the Table, and The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten.

I'm Norman Swan and I'll see you soon.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a subject close to all of our hearts, food. And in particular,
the politics of food. It was a discussion I chaired at this year's Sydney Writers
Festival. And before we got going I was fascinated to know what the audience's
attitudes were to food, and I found that most of them were on a gluten-free diet,
and a large proportion were watching their carbs.

Anyway, on the panel were Indira Naidoo, author of The Edible Balcony and The
Edible City, Damon Gameau, author of That Sugar Book and producer and host
of That Sugar Film, and Julian Baggini, a British philosopher and prolific writer,
including The Virtues of the Table and The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten.

What do you think about people being food focused, Julian? You've got strong
opinions about that.

Julian Baggini: Well, I don't have strong opinions…

Norman Swan: Well, you wrote a book about it.

Julian Baggini: Yes, I did write a book about it, yeah. My philosophical
influences are people like Aristotle and David Hume who actually had very little to
say about food. But if you go to Aristotle, Aristotle advocated this doctrine of the
mean, which is actually funnily enough Confucius also advocated something
similar, and that way of looking at things says that generally speaking the
extremist positions tend to be wrong, and the appropriate thing is something
between.

I think the Western philosophical tradition has tended to be really down on food
and on the body and tended to think that anyone who pays any attention to it at
all is kind of deluded. You know, they are just like animals because animals eat,
so if you focus on eating you're like an animal. Brillat-Savarin, the French food
writer, said animals feed and humans eat. Food is a very important part of life. It's
part of what makes us human, it's very humanising, and it connects us to all sorts
of important issues.

At the same time though, to become obsessive about food, there are certain food
obsessions that I think are legitimate. You know, if you are a really creative chef,
for example, or you are a really great producer of food, that's your obsession, but

there are unhealthy obsessions around food, for sure. So it's about finding the
appropriate balance for it in life, the appropriate place for it. It's neither everything
nor nothing.

Norman Swan: The Edible City is all about bringing people together around
food, isn't it.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, it is, and I'm certainly of the school of thought…the first thing
I think about what I wake up in the morning is what I'm going to eat, and the last
thing I think about is what I'm going to eat the next day…

Norman Swan: And in between times? Is there any time you don't think about
food?

Indira Naidoo: I tend to eat about two or three times a day. But for me, food is
much more than a really important part of our life. One of the tragedies we've
fallen into in the Western modern way of looking at food is that it's something
we've developed these paranoias about. 'Oh my God, what is that going to do to
me if I eat that?' And so that has been a really concerning because for me it's a
joyous experience. Food is joyous to eat. The anticipation of food, the sharing of
food, the actual process of eating it and then the discussion around it. So for me
it's a sad day when food isn't the central part of the day. And I think that that is
where it has become really disturbing, is that it's this also-ran thing, this thing I
just pick up on the way or pull out a packet or pour something out of a tin or a
container. I think that that's where the problems have become, that we have
reduced food rather than elevated it to where it should be.

Norman Swan: But do you think Damon has reduced food and created all sorts
of paranoia through his bestselling books?

Damon Gameau: You can answer honestly, it's fine.

Norman Swan: Do you think so?

Indira Naidoo: Look, I think in terms of the Damon's work and Damon's book,
obviously I'm very concerned about the amount of sugar in our diet and I think
that it is a big problem. We are eating something like 1,000% more sugar than
we did 200 years ago. It's leading to lots of disease and wellness issues.

Norman Swan: What are you going to do about your desert menus if you
abandon sugar?

Indira Naidoo: Well, I think that we went through the stage when we demonised
fat, we went through the stage when we demonised protein, and I think that we
have to be aware that there are some things we need to have in moderation, like
sugar. But you can't look at food in terms of just its nutrients, you have to look at
it holistically, look at the apple, not just look at it as a sum of proteins and
nutrients and fats and sugars. And I think that that is where we are going a little
wrong.

Norman Swan: So Damon, I've got a bone to pick with you…

Damon Gameau: Pick away.

Norman Swan: Last night I tried one of your recipes. I almost sliced my finger
chopping broccoli.

Damon Gameau: Oh, so I'm to blame! You need to improve your culinary skills.

Norman Swan: I do, refine that technique. Were you surprised by the polling of
the audience in terms of the food obsessions in the audience or food interest?

Damon Gameau: Well, I think we've got to be very careful, I think what we are in
the middle of at the moment is the food revolution where people are starting to
empower themselves with information about food. I don't necessarily think that's
a bad thing as long as it stays in a safe area. I think we have been misled for 35
years in a lot of different ways. I think the environment has supported companies
making enormous amount of profit telling us what to eat and shaping their
marketing strategies to get us hooked on these kind of products.

And certainly where I come from is that we don't think sugar per se is bad or evil,
we are trying to get people to say, look, the World Health Organisation
recommends about six teaspoons of sugar a day. Our teenagers are having
about 40 teaspoons. So clearly there is a lack of understanding with the food
supply. So how do we teach people those skills to raise their awareness, learn to
read labels, understand what they are putting in their bodies, because I think now
the science tells us not only the physical symptoms but your mental, your vitality,

your emotions are determined by the foods you are eating. If we can get this
through to kids we're going to set them up for a much healthier lifestyle. And
that's not to say that we demonise these foods, we just get them to take
responsibility and understand what they are putting in their bodies.

Norman Swan: So do you think that you can actually counter the effect of the
globalised food industry?

Damon Gameau: Well, I think we are going to have to because the reality is we
are using nearly 40% of our land now for farming, we are going to be 9 billion
people by 2050, we need to rethink the way we approach food, and I think that's
going to switch us back to local. We are going to have to teach kids about
growing their own vegetables because we can't keep going the way we are. So
we need people to understand food a bit more.

I think the key with sugar is that we forget that sugar is not a nutrient. There is no
biological requirement for added sugar in our diet. We can get all the sugar we
need from fruits and vegetables and other sources. So as a treat, fantastic, every
now and again. But we've got to a point where it is now in 80% of the food supply
and most people are having 30 or 40 teaspoons a day. That's not a treat any
more, that has kind of tipped the balance, and that's why we are seeing this
catastrophic health crisis.

Julian Baggini: Yes, because there's not really a food industry…because I think
sometimes the food industry is presented as this huge, big, all-powerful demon
which excites huge control over us, and of course there have been abuses. And
Damon's film points to the way in which there has been some misinformation and
deliberate suppression of information about the health of this food. So clearly I'm
not saying they are blameless, but I think that the danger of putting that kind of
view of the food industry is it makes it seem like we are less powerful than we
are. And also we got to remember at the end of the day they are about making
money. At the end of the day it's consumer demand. When consumers start
demanding organic, they stock the organic. When they want reduced sugar, they
stock reduced sugar. So they are not going to foist these things upon us if we
don't willingly take them. With more information, we make our choices, the food
industry will respond.

Norman Swan: But isn't that a bit naive because what we have is a saturated fat
mountain, we have a sugar mountain. All the food that people don't eat gets put
into a mountain and then put into high calorie, low value foods. There is a degree
of dumping and creation of markets too.

Julian Baggini: Well, there is, but remember, people aren't entirely powerless
about that, except…and this is where it gets very interesting, the politics…of
course where people are poor, where there is not enough money. So I think in
developed countries most people actually have the resources to eat proper good
food, it's often not more expensive if you know where to get it. But let's be
honest, generally speaking you do have to pay a bit to get the quality stuff. Most
people can afford that, they choose other priorities, it's as simple as that. But
there's always that 10%, 20% of people in countries like Australia, in Britain, who
have very little money, and those are the people who have very little choice but
to buy those processed products with all these things in it. So that's where the
politics I think it gets more tricky.

Indira Naidoo: I agree with Julian in terms of the food companies do respond to
consumers. I mean, in the end they are there to make money, and if consumers
want a particular product with a particular composition, they will respond to it. We
have seen examples of that here in Australia. My concern is when consumers
show that they want a certain product…for instance, we are having a big debate
in Australia at the moment with our free range eggs. Consumers have shown that
they want free range eggs but they want them to be labelled accurately. And
unfortunately the policy makers aren't helping consumers make that decision. So
eggs are being labelled as free range when…

Norman Swan: They are just in a larger cage.

Indira Naidoo: Exactly, 10,000 chickens to a shed instead of the 1,500, which is
the code. This makes it really hard for consumers. They want to do the right
thing, they want to buy free range, but they are presented with a product that
clearly is not. And what that does is the people who are doing the right thing, the
egg farmers who are doing the right thing, looking after those animals well and
delivering a free range product, are getting messed up in the caged hens and the
limited access to outdoor pasture. So that's why for me it needs to be a two-
pronged approach. Consumers, yes, say we now have got the information, this is

what we want. The companies say, okay, we will respond to that. But the
policymakers have to make sure that those regulations are enforced and the
people who do the wrong thing are punished.

Damon Gameau: And the problem in Australia that we found with the film is
that…we've had two UK parliamentary screenings, New Zealand parliamentary
screening, we had two scheduled in Australia, and not one politician turned up,
didn't even send an intern. I got to go and meet one of the ministers, and we are
the second biggest exporter of sugar in the world, so it's kind of a don't-go-there
topic. And at the same time, look, there are a host of factors that are contributing
to the diseases we're seeing but sugar is a major factor, especially around kids,
that if they had the gumption to actually take some…I agree, it's part empowering
the consumer but also the government need to help out in some way, whether it's
regulating the companies, but they need to take action.

Norman Swan: So it has been said that big food is acting like a big tobacco now.
One of the things that we know works with tobacco, and particularly in children, is
price. Where do you stand on a sugar tax?

Damon Gameau: Well, I guess the only working model of it so far has come out
of Mexico and it has now been 18 months, they put a levy on sugary drinks,
they've seen a 17% reduction in their lower socio-economic areas. But more
importantly they've raised $1.8 billion. So the only way I would support it (and I
don't think this is going to happen) is if we set up a transparent independent body
that said, all right, with that money raised, let's use it to subsidise fresh fruits and
vegetables, let's revamp our hospital system and our schools and give them
fresh, affordable foods. But unfortunately I don't think we are going to see that
happen, it's going to disappear into the coffers.

Norman Swan: A new submarine in South Australia.

Damon Gameau: There you go, yes.

Norman Swan: But then people will say it's the Nanny State. People have got
control over their lives, Julian, let it be.

Julian Baggini: Nanny State arguments are very easy to make. The fact of the
matter is that we support regulation of all sorts of things for our mutual benefit. It

is not a nanny because if the restrictions are there with the consent and the
approval and demand of the populace, it is something we choose together, it's
not about the state saying 'you can't do that'. But also I think the other problem
with the Nanny State argument is we've got to remember that the people who
make that case, imagine that there is something out there which is called the
pure free market which is operating independently of any government on policy
issues, and that that is sufficient. That is not the case and it never has been the
case. We have the kind of foods we have in the proportion we have them at the
price we have them for all sorts of very complicated issues around agricultural
subsidy, trade tariffs and so forth. The food supply system is saturated in policy
and law and regulation. So when someone says what we are going to do is we
want to change a part of that to get slightly better results, you're not introducing
an intervention which wasn't there before, you are simply changing what exactly
is being intervened about. So it's perfectly legitimate.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, I agree absolutely. We do tend to forget that government
policy has led us to where we are in our food system at the moment. It hasn't
happened separate to government policy, they have been actively intervening in
that process over the last 10, 20, 30 years. And also too you've got to remember
that the food companies are actively intervening as well. Every couple of months
they are changing compositions of foods to amp up sugar or amp up salt or fat.
So the whole system…it's not that you are just being given a product that just sits
there and hasn't been changed in a number of decades, everyone involved in this
process is changing compositions. And unfortunately in terms of government
policy and health policy we've been lagging behind, we have not been keeping
up with how willing big business is to change the composition of foods to make it
almost impossible not to be addictive. Our brains love salt, fat and sugar. Who in
this room doesn't love that!

Norman Swan: You're listening to a discussion on the politics of food from this
year's Sydney Writers Festival. On the panel are Indira Naidoo, Damon Gameau,
and philosopher Julian Baggini.

I want to get back to a comment that Damon made right at the beginning which is
the back to the earth idea of growing your own food, which you give I think four
examples in The Edible City, a couple in Melbourne and Sydney, Wayside
Chapel and so on. But to what extent is it scalable? We are trying to limit the size

of our cities, lose the quarter-acre block, live in apartments. I know you've got the
balcony idea. But nonetheless, how practical is it that we can get back in touch
with our food?

Indira Naidoo: I think we really need to. We have all become grossly
disconnected from our food. And the groups I particularly work with are the ones
that are suffering most from this new food world. You know, they are poor,
disadvantaged, homeless, newly arrived immigrants, asylum seekers, elderly,
retired, kids in school. So they are the people unfortunately that so many of these
bad products are being directed at. And what I found from my work is when you
help these communities reconnect with their food, even if it's just growing a few
pots of herbs on their balcony or on the stairwell or if they have a balcony or a a
little garden, that process of seeing how something grows, to see a piece of fruit,
to see a lettuce, a cabbage, an apple actually grow, has been quite
transformative for so many of these communities because something like 60% of
our diet…

Norman Swan: But in the end it's cheaper to buy something from the burger
shop down the road.

Indira Naidoo: Well, you have to educate people about what cheap actually
means. And I think that we've gone through an era where we expect food to be
cheap, but what we don't understand is that so many of the external costs of that
food haven't actually been priced into the cost of that food.

Norman Swan: So the food miles, the transportation…

Indira Naidoo: That's right. So a McDonald's hamburger may cost three dollars,
but when you look at the food miles, the environmental aspect, the low wages
paid to workers, the cost of pollution, whatever it might be, if you really put all
those costs into the value of the hamburger, actually the average person
probably wouldn't be able to afford it.

Norman Swan: But isn't that slightly naive because you should have it costed
into the price of the hamburger but it's not, and if you haven't got much money
then that's what your money goes on.

Indira Naidoo: Absolutely. I mean, I'm not someone who is anti-hamburgers
particularly, but it's about what you help people get access to. And in the suburbs
I work in, sometimes fast food is the only thing they have. There's no grocery
stores, not even a general supermarket. So you have to work within that. But
once you introduce that sense that they can have a little bit of autonomy, see
how food grows, what it takes to grow food, it starts making them think differently.
So when you buy an eggplant for 5c or 10c at the supermarket and it has taken
you three months to grow it, you ask different questions as a conscious
consumer and eater than you would as just a consumer. And I think that that is
part of the process. Obviously no one is going to be able to grow all the food they
need when you live in urban environments in cities, but we can certainly grow
much more of our food, we can localise it much more, make it more nutritious
and more accessible, and also cheaper.

Our homeless community in the Wayside Chapel in Potts Point I work with, 200
square metres on that rooftop we grow vegetables, we have five or six beehives
producing honey. And when our homeless visitors arrive in the garden every
Thursday for garden class, the first thing they do is literally eat the garden. That
is their meal of the day. And the first time that happened it really blew me away
because obviously they don't have the income to buy nutritious food, and for
them that vegetable garden is their supermarket.

Norman Swan: So how to do these adjustments, Damon?

Damon Gameau: I kind of agree with Indira in the sense that we are not going to
have a choice. I think we are going to have to switch to this kind of micro farming,
food towers, we are going to have to start growing more local. And the
Worldwatch Institute did a report that said that 80% of New York residents could
be fed from rooftop gardens. And the way we are heading, the impact on our
food and our apples being shipped from London to South Africa to be polished
and then shipped back to the UK to be sold, it's absolutely mad. We need to find
a way to promote local eating again. And, as Indira was saying, I think a burger
should be reflective of what its true value is in terms of those miles. So if you
want a hamburger, great, but it's going to be $11. But if you want the local
banana, is going to be 40c because…

Norman Swan: So that implies differential taxation by governments.

Damon Gameau: Well, I think it's inevitable. We don't realise the impact of
what's happening to our climate. I don't think people understand how food is
going to be affected in the next 40 to 50 years. We are going to have to make
some fundamental decisions around that because we cannot keep going the way
we are. So I think the more we can force people to try and grow their own, have
these community gardens, it's going to help.

Julian Baggini: I've got reservations about all of this. I think that it's always good
to grow food for various reasons, not mainly around self-sufficiency I would say
actually, to do with other things, connection and stuff. But I think there's a bit of a
danger of turning this local thing into a kind of religion, and it doesn't add up
actually. I think there are really good things about eating things that are not
remotely local, for all sorts of reasons. First of all, I grew up in a time where the
progressive view was always one of internationalism and connections with other
people, and I think that part of the way we have food from all around the world is
part of that more cosmopolitan, outward looking thing. And I worry in Britain
sometimes…

Norman Swan: Not many mango trees in Glasgow, I can tell you.

Julian Baggini: No, exactly. And so sometimes this 'go local' thing in Britain,
what bothers me is it is happening as a cultural phenomenon at about the same
sort of time where people are also talking about closing the borders, keeping the
immigrants out et cetera. It's the benign side, it can be, not always, an element of
it is a benign side of a kind of provincialism. But also on environmental grounds
it's not as straightforward as 'local is better'.

Interesting reports done on New Zealand's products, New Zealand has lamb and
butter and everything. They can produce it with a very low carbon footprint
because they've got the perfect environment for it. And shipping is a very, very
low carbon way of transferring things. The total carbon footprint of something
grown in optimal conditions and shipped very far distance can be less than
something grown locally where you have to put a lot of synthetic inputs, artificial
heating, greenhouses and so forth.

So I'm all for lots of getting back in touch with the local and supporting it and
certainly avoiding foods which carry this very, very heavy carbon footprint, but it's

just too simplistic to think that everything that has travelled a long way has a
heavy carbon footprint. It doesn't. Bananas are great. And bananas, they don't
grow here, we put them in ships, low carbon footprint, delicious, nutritious. And,
even when fair trade, not very expensive.

Damon Gameau: How do you think that looks when we have 10 billion people in
2050 and an estimated 28 billion by the end of the century? How do we deal with
those trade routes and shipping? If we are still existing as we are now, what are
the implications for the planet?

Julian Baggini: Well, they will have to be changes for various reasons, as the
one you pointed out. But I think the solution for our food security is not to reduce
our interdependence. We are going to become more interdependent. In a
globalised world it's even more important that we trade in ways that are efficient,
that we grow things where they grow best and most efficiently, and where we can
transport them with a low carbon footprint we can. If we try and grow everything
local to us, then what's going to happen is that people who are blessed with the
climates and everything that they can do that will do well, and other people are
going to starve, so we have to make these adjustments.

Norman Swan: Let's try this bit of moral calculus on you. So the National Party in
Australia, the country party, objects, by and large, to foreign interests buying our
farming land. A huge debate over a very large livestock holding recently which
the government caved in on and said, well, they couldn't buy it with the way it
was structured. And the theory here is that, well, dairy produce, meat produce is
going to be grown and sent straight to China, and then we might be having a
problem with food security. What's the moral calculus around this? Have the
Chinese got a right to buy our agricultural land, export directly to China, in a
growing world which, if Damon is right, we're going to need every scrap of food
we can get?

Julian Baggini: Look, there are lots of issues tied up in that. When it comes to
land ownership we have a system where people can privately own land, but it
doesn't mean that once you've paid for it it's yours and you can do what you like
with it. Without knowing the ins and outs of this particular debate, who owns it or
not in a legal contract isn't really the key issue. The main thing is there are
regulations in any given country about how land is used so it's used in a

sustainable and fair way and it benefits everybody and it benefits the people here
as well.

Indira Naidoo: This debate has concerned me a little because I find sometimes
it's a little racist. It's always the Chinese. And there are a lot of other foreign
investors who are buying up Australian land and Australian dairies and
agricultural land. So I'd like to see just more about foreign interests rather than a
particular nationality.

But I think this is the important thing about the education process about growing
food, is that you see the importance of our food producers and our growers in the
system. And again, when you are an urban consumer going to the supermarket,
you are not really thinking about where that food comes from, who has grown it,
who has put all that effort into it. And when you grow an eggplant and you
understand the time, the effort, the commitment, the people who do that fulltime
become your heroes. And I think that this debate hopefully is repositioning our
farmers in a more positive and strong light, because without them, who is going
to grow our food?

Norman Swan: So we are seeing a dairy crisis as we speak?

Indira Naidoo: We are.

Norman Swan: Julian sits on an organisation called the Food Ethics Council in
the UK and they talk about a square deal for farmers. Do you think we are giving
Australian farmers a square deal?

Indira Naidoo: No, of course not. I mean, we are seeing the death of our rural
communities, farmers now walking off the land. We are seeing hugely high
suicide rates amongst our farming community. I think it's devastating. I don't
know how farmers are hanging in there. But I think we need to bridge this urban
and rural gap that we've got at the moment. And I think food and understanding
the importance of it and how important that food is going to become for our
future…Australia is becoming more and more climate challenged. We have only
got a really thin fertile strip around the edge of our country to grow food, and the
people who can do it well and do it productively are really key to the future of our
country.

Damon Gameau: Yes, I think a symptom of that too is that most people are
unaware that I think 80c of every dollar that Australians spend goes to either
Coles or Woollies, whether it's through food, alcohol, gambling, petrol. So it's
almost a dictatorship in a way. And I think because of that impact, the way they
can affect the farmers there…I've met a farmer who grows lettuce, and he said
his quota that he has to provide every month is 1,000 tonnes of lettuce. Now, he
has to grow that amount every single month. If a company only wants 400
tonnes, then that 600 tonnes gets thrown out. So the system is just so
unproductive the way we are doing it at the moment, and this is where we need
to rethink how we are approaching this. And ultimately it's probably a systemic
problem that, as you said, we've designed a system that…

Norman Swan: But in the end it's a market and in the end you've got to change
the way the the market works. So tell me how you would change…

Indira Naidoo: But I think you've also got to help consumers make a much more
informed question. I worked at Choice, a consumer advocacy group, and I was
really fascinated by the main question that consumers ask themselves when they
go into a shop; how much does something cost. That was their first question.

Norman Swan: And if you talk to Coles and Woollies, that's what they say, it's
price, price, price.

Indira Naidoo: Yes, and obviously it is not always the best question. And so
what I hope we can help people do is ask the other questions they need to ask;
why does it cost that, why doesn't it cost this, who has made it, what's gone into
it, how has it been produced, how are those animals being treated? There are a
whole lot of other questions. When you get a litre of milk the same or cheaper
than a litre of water, you know something has gone wrong. As a consumer you
shouldn't go, 'yay, that's fantastic', you should say 'someone has been screwed-
over here'.

Norman Swan: And it's the water buyers! Damon, how do you square your view
about food miles with, if you like, social justice across nations where coffee
producers, cocoa producers, and increasingly others…as sub-Saharan Africa
gets a bit richer, they'll start producing grain and other things, drought

allowing…don't they have a right to sell their products on an international market
and ship them to distant places?

Damon Gameau: Of course, and I think what we are losing here is we are
switching to extremities. We are not saying that suddenly we stop all trade and
shipping. If there are certain things that still require that and they are available at
a certain price because they are a special, yes, absolutely. But like I said, when
we are shipping apples between countries for no reason other than the polishing,
I think there's a broken system there, because it's cheaper to do that for them
than do it within their own country, that's the issue we need to address.

Norman Swan: But what I'm losing here in this discussion is (I'm sorry, I'm being
boring and practical) how are you adjust the market so that it's different for
apples from coffee.

Julian Baggini: Look, it is really, really difficult, I think this is true. The thing
about the market system, the so-called perfection of the market, is that there is a
lot of truth involved in it. One reason why it's good to have trade is that it's more
efficient for some people to do a lot of one thing rather than everyone doing
everything themselves. An apple tree in every garden is not as efficient as an
orchard from which we all take things. So there is no simple answer. Food is also
complicated because supply is not easily switched on and off because there are
all sorts of things to do with the weather and the seasons this year and
everything. So getting it perfectly right is very difficult.

I think the point is you shouldn't be seduced by the idea of what would the perfect
system look like. I think we can see lots of examples already where systems
have emerged for various usually political reasons which just have bizarre and
perverse consequences…

Norman Swan: Such as?

Julian Baggini: Subsidies, for example, for grain. It is particularly bad in
America. America subsidises the production of certain crops…

Norman Swan: Fructose is the classic one.

Julian Baggini: Yes, exactly, which creates this glut of fructose which means it
has to be put into everything and corn syrup and everything. So there are lots of
perverse incentives there. And there is also not the right kind of taxation. We put
taxation on things and we have very crude categories for this. You know, luxury
goods get sales tax in the UK, basic foodstuffs don't. But what fits into what
category? It varies.

So I think in a way there is nothing really simple and inspiring that we can say
about this. We have to go ad hoc, bit by bit, changing this bit of regulation, that
regulation, trying to nudge ourselves towards something, and also having the
humility to realise that this is a bit experimental. Markets and food supply
systems are extremely complicated and there's always the risk of unintentionally
having a perverse outcome.

People with perfectly good intentions…in the EU for example, after the Second
World War the EU decided it had to make sure it never got close to starvation
again because during the war lots of people got close to starvation. So it had
these agricultural policies designed to create food security, but because they
were, in retrospect, badly designed, it just created the butter lakes, the milk
lakes, the butter mountains. So we've got to have the humility to realise that we
may well get things like this wrong. But you've got to at least start with an
awareness of what the proper problem is and what we are trying to get towards.
And I think at the moment, up until now perhaps too much has been based on
the idea…the main incentive is to keep things cheap and that's it.

Norman Swan: That was part of a discussion on the politics of food that I chaired
at this year's Writers Festival. You were listening to Indira Naidoo, author of The
Edible Balcony and The Edible City, Damon Gameau, author of That Sugar
Book and That Sugar Film, and Julian Baggini, a British philosopher and prolific
writer, including The Virtues of the Table, and The Pig That Wants to Be Eaten.

I'm Norman Swan and I'll see you soon.
